title: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
subtitle: Fix the alkalosis first, then the pylorus

sources.title: Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Vomiting in infants (J Am Coll Radiol 2020;17(11S):S505-S515)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people in hospital (NG29)
Open versus laparoscopic pyloromyotomy for pyloric stenosis (Staerkle et al, CD012827)

red_flags.text: Bilious vomiting. That is not pyloric stenosis and needs the bilious vomiting pathway now.
A lethargic, poorly perfused infant with a sunken fontanelle and dry nappies: severe dehydration.
Apnoeas or hypoventilation in a markedly alkalotic infant. Metabolic alkalosis depresses respiratory drive, and it gets worse after a general anaesthetic.
Jaundice or hypoglycaemia in a starved, vomiting infant.

do_now.text: Stop feeds, site intravenous access and send a capillary or venous blood gas with chloride, sodium, potassium and glucose.
Shocked infant: isotonic crystalloid bolus at the NICE NG29 volume, reassessing after each bolus.
Start isotonic maintenance fluid containing glucose, with potassium added once the infant is passing urine, per local paediatric protocol.
Pyloromyotomy is never an emergency. It waits until the alkalosis and hypochloraemia are corrected, however long that takes.

assess.text: Typical infant is a few weeks old with non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and remains hungry. A family history is common.
Weigh the infant and assess hydration. Compare with the birth weight.
Test feed: palpate for the olive in the right upper quadrant with the stomach empty and the infant settled. Look for visible gastric peristalsis.

investigate.text: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice: measure pyloric muscle thickness and channel length, and watch for failure of the pylorus to open. Interpret against the radiology department's thresholds.
Blood gas: the classic picture is hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Repeat it to guide correction rather than guessing.
Upper GI contrast study only if ultrasound is non-diagnostic or another diagnosis such as malrotation is suspected.

resuscitate.text: Correct over 24 to 48 hours as needed with isotonic sodium chloride containing glucose and potassium. Re-check the gas and electrolytes regularly.
Proceed to surgery only once chloride and bicarbonate are within the ranges set by local paediatric anaesthetic protocol. The anaesthetist sets the bar, not the list.
Nasogastric tube is optional in a stable infant; replace large gastric losses volume for volume with isotonic fluid if one is placed.

definitive.text: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, open or laparoscopic, on a planned list after correction. Both approaches are acceptable; laparoscopy may carry a slightly higher risk of incomplete myotomy.
Before the anaesthetic, the anaesthetist empties the stomach with a nasogastric tube. These infants have full stomachs regardless of fasting time.
After surgery, resume feeding early on an ad-libitum or short graded regimen per unit protocol. Some post-operative vomiting is expected and is not a failed operation.

escalate.text: Transfer to a paediatric surgical unit for the operation. Resuscitation and correction should start before transfer, not after.
Paediatric anaesthetic involvement from the start: post-operative apnoea is a real risk in a young, alkalotic, or ex-premature infant.
Persistent vomiting beyond the first few post-operative days suggests incomplete myotomy or a missed perforation; discuss with the operating surgeon.

notes: The chloride is the number that tells you when this baby is safe for theatre. Sodium and potassium matter, but the chloride drives correction of the alkalosis.
A surgeon who takes an uncorrected alkalotic infant to theatre risks a baby who does not breathe adequately afterwards.
Projectile, non-bilious, hungry, a few weeks old: pattern recognition is strong here, but ultrasound confirms it.
